cues.text: Around 1380, a priest named Fr. Eligius van der Aker was celebrating Mass at the altar of the Three Kings in Boxtel , in the southern Netherlands.
Immediately after the consecration, he accidentally knocked over the chalice containing the consecrated wine.

The spilled wine, tradition holds, immediately turned to blood and stained both the corporal beneath the chalice and the larger altar cloth — a transformation witnesses present recognized at once as something beyond an ordinary accidental spill.

The most authoritative surviving document describing the event is a decree issued in 1380 itself by Cardinal Pileus, confirming the sign within the same year it occurred — an unusually swift ecclesiastical response for a medieval Eucharistic account.
A Relic Shared Between Two Towns
The blood-stained corporal has remained in Boxtel ever since, while the larger altar cloth was given to neighboring Hoogstraten .
The town lies just across what is now the Belgian border, with both towns sharing one devotion divided between two relics from that year forward.
Pilgrims traveled to Boxtel to venerate the Heilig Bloed, the Holy Blood, from shortly after the event onward, and the town's devotion to the relic has continued for well over six centuries.

The sign remains, in local memory, a reminder that even a priest's ordinary clumsiness at the altar could become, in a single moment, an occasion the whole of two neighboring towns would choose to remember.
